title: NAVIGATING THROUGH PAUL'S LETTERS: WALK THROUGH OF ROMANS 5

sense.text: “even as our beloved brother Paul also according to the wisdom given unto him hath written unto you”. Peter is giving kudos and respect to Paul for the wisdom that was in him. That wisdom is Christ, the spirit of Christ. Peter acknowledged the spirit of the Lord in Paul when Paul wrote his letters, and he wrote that acknowledgment down.

“in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction.” Why their own destruction? Because they take Paul’s letters and twist them to teach a whole different gospel.

The other scriptures are the law and the prophets, the Old Testament, the scriptures Paul cites. They stumble because they do not know the other scriptures, and they think Paul was just writing things out of thin air. To understand Paul’s letters, you must understand the other scriptures.

When people don’t understand Paul’s letters, they start saying Paul is not really authoritative. They speak evil of dignities, and say the same of Mark and Luke because they were not of the twelve. When you speak evil of dignities, your mind is blinded, and Satan takes over and has you teaching a whole different gospel: that nations can be saved, teaching them about heaven while you are in their hell. Those that do that are house negroes, the worst kind of negro.

“Ye therefore, beloved, seeing ye know these things before”: you know beforehand that the unlearned and unstable twist Paul’s letters. “beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness.”

The error of the wicked comes from those that wrest the other scriptures and Paul’s letters. When you start teaching that your oppressor can be granted the same benefits as you, that the nations can receive some twisted salvation of some kind, you are in the error of the wicked. It is a whole different gospel.

“To all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints”. Paul is writing to the saints at Rome. Some Christians say he is writing to Israelites and other nations at the same time. No: the letter is addressed to the saints at Rome.

Is he addressing both Jews and Gentiles in the church? Yes. But they are all saints. Other nations are never referred to as saints, so Paul is not writing to other nations at all.

precepts.why:
“He also exalteth the horn of his people, the praise of all his saints; even of the children of Israel, a people near unto him.” The people near unto him are the saints. The children of Israel are the saints: we are the saints.

So when Paul writes to those in Rome “called to be saints”, he is writing to the children of Israel in Rome.

“Behold, thou art called a Jew, and restest in the law, and makest thy boast of God”. Paul is writing to the Jews. There is obviously northern kingdom in the congregations there as well, but he is writing to Judah, to the Jews. That settles who the letter is addressed to.

“Know ye not, brethren, (for I speak to them that know the law,)”. He speaks to them that know the law because he is writing to Jews, “how that the law hath dominion over a man as long as he liveth”.

So Paul is writing to Jews, to them that know the law, to the saints at Rome. That is who Paul is writing to.

sense.text:
This is Paul’s source material. “Having therefore obtained help of God, I continue unto this day, witnessing both to small and great, saying none other things than those which the prophets and Moses did say should come”. Paul was only teaching what Moses and the prophets said.

That is why Peter mentions the other scriptures. People stumble because they believe Paul was writing things out of thin air. To understand Paul’s letters you must understand the other scriptures, because Paul taught from nothing else than what was written in the law and in the prophets.

precepts.why:
“to whom he expounded and testified the kingdom of God, persuading them concerning Jesus, both out of the law of Moses, and out of the prophets, from morning till evening.” Paul was teaching out of the law and the prophets, so his letters are based on the law and the prophets. He was not sitting around making things up.

Are there places where the spirit of Christ spoke through Paul and things were added? Yes. But 99.9% of Paul’s letters is the law and the prophets, and a small part is like the unbelieving wife departing. That is not found in Moses, because under Moses, if you did not believe, you were put to death. If your wife believed in Satan in the wilderness and you believed in the Lord, she got death. That was added for that time.

That is the difference, and that is why Peter speaks of the wisdom given unto him: that is Christ speaking through Paul.

sense.text:
“What shall we say then that Abraham our father, as pertaining to the flesh, hath found?” All nations do not have Abraham as their father, so Paul cannot have been writing to all nations. Some Christians say “our father” means by faith. No: our father means by race, by ancestry. The saints Paul writes to are Abraham’s children by descent.

Romans 5 is the last safe haven Christianity has. John 3:16, Galatians 3:28, Romans 11 and Acts 10 have already been conquered. Romans 5 is difficult, and it is their last strong tower, but it has got to come down. And Romans 5 has to be read from Romans 4, because it is all one letter.

“For if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God.” Focus on the word justified, because it comes up again and again. The works are sacrifice. Did Abraham sacrifice early in Genesis? Yes. But his belief, his faith, came first. Faith precedes the works.

If Abraham were justified by works, he could glory because he sacrificed, but not before God. The Lord counted Abraham righteous on his belief, because his belief went before his works, and his works followed.

“For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.” What does the scripture say about works? Abraham had faith, and his faith was counted for righteousness; the works followed the faith. That is how Paul quotes Genesis 15: faith first, then works.

The context is that Paul is writing to Jews who were born and raised in the law, who believed their works were enough. When Paul wrote to them they were still going to the temple and still sacrificing. Paul is telling them: you cannot boast in animal sacrifice; that is not enough anymore. You have to have faith in Christ first and foremost.

“Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt.” To him that works, that offers sacrifices, the reward is not reckoned of grace, or mercy, but of debt. The debt is the law of sacrifice: under sacrifice you are indebted to sacrifice an animal or die. Under Moses there was no mercy and no grace.

The prophets spoke of the temple being destroyed. Once the temple is destroyed, what happens to your works? If your faith is based solely on sacrificing an animal and the temple is gone, where does your faith go? You are screwed. If you indebted yourself to sacrificing animals as your atonement and the temple is gone, you have condemned yourself already, because there is no animal, no priest and no temple to atone with. So Paul tells them their faith has to supersede the works.

“But to him that worketh not”: him that does not offer sacrifice, “but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly”: him that has faith in Christ, who justifies the ungodly through his death. “his faith is counted for righteousness”, just as Abraham’s was before he sacrificed. Believeth and faith are synonymous.

While the temple was still standing the argument was: what justifies us, the animals or Christ’s body? Paul had to clear it up with the Jews in Rome, who were still going to the temple. Sacrifice all you want, but if you make your salvation rest on animal sacrifice, you are indebted to it as long as that temple is around, and once it is destroyed you are done. You have to have faith on Christ. That is the context of Romans 4: faith before the works.

“Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works”. God imputed righteousness to Abraham without the works of sacrifice. The Lord had already acknowledged Abraham’s faith before he sacrificed animals; Abraham was deemed faithful before he ever sacrificed.

precepts.why:
This is the scripture Paul quotes, and it shows what the works were. “Fear not, Abram: I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward.” Abram answers, “what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless, and the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus?” Abraham was too old and Sarah was too old to have children, so he said the oldest servant of his house would be his heir: “lo, one born in my house is mine heir.”

“This shall not be thine heir; but he that shall come forth out of thine own bowels shall be thine heir.” Eliezer will not be your heir; you are going to have a son in your old age. “Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them: and he said unto him, So shall thy seed be.” You are going to have a lot of children.

“And he believed in the Lord; and he counted it to him for righteousness.” An old man is told by the Lord that he will have a child in his old age, and he believed it. That right there is Abraham’s faith. The Lord said it, Abraham believed it. Belief goes back to faith.

Then the Lord says, “I am the Lord that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give thee this land to inherit it”, and Abraham asks, “whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it?” He believed the Lord when he promised him an heir, and he believed the Lord when he promised him the promised land.

Only after that: “Take me an heifer of three years old, and a she goat of three years old, and a ram of three years old, and a turtledove, and a young pigeon.” He “divided them in the midst, and laid each piece one against another: but the birds divided he not.” What is Abraham doing here? Sacrificing. What came first? The faith came first, then the works. That is why Paul quoted this: faith has to precede the works.

What are the works Paul means by “him that worketh”? Peter said they stumble at the other scriptures, and these are the scriptures Paul cites from. There are many verses that say what the works are; this one condenses it into one verse.

“For the shewbread, and for the continual meat offering, and for the continual burnt offering, of the sabbaths, of the new moons, for the set feasts, and for the holy things, and for the sin offerings to make an atonement for Israel”. Continual: done all the time, daily, yearly. To make an atonement goes back to the word justify: atone, justify and reconcile are completely the same thing.

“and for all the work of the house of our God.” That is the works Paul is talking about: temple sacrifice, the temple law. Knowing that, no one coming to the camp can confound you at Romans 4.

On grace: “He that despised Moses’ law died without mercy under two or three witnesses”. Without mercy means without grace. If you did not keep what you were indebted to keep, you got death.

There were things an animal could not atone for. If you broke the Sabbath, you could not atone with an animal. Homosexuality, you could not atone with an animal. Idolatry, you could not atone with an animal: you had to die. And if you chose not to sacrifice at all, you had to die.

So under Moses, under the sacrificial law, we were indebted to offer continual sacrifices all the time: continual burnt offerings, drink offerings, sin offerings. That is the debt of Romans 4:4, reward “not reckoned of grace, but of debt.”

sense.text: “And being not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sara’s womb”. Sarah could not have children: she was ninety years old, and her womb was dead.

“He staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief”. He was promised the land, and he did not live on it long; he was old and he died. But he did not doubt that his wife would bring forth a child at ninety. He did not need to sacrifice an animal to believe it; he believed it off top. He did not say, You sure, Lord? How do you know? He was like Moses, meek, completely submissive to the Lord: understood, Lord. “but was strong in faith, giving glory to God”: strong in belief.

“And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform.” He was fully persuaded that his children would be as the sand of the sea and as the stars of heaven. Did he live to see it? No, but he believed it. He was told he would have a child in his old age; he believed it, and it happened. He understood that what the Lord promised, God was able to perform.

“And therefore it was imputed to him for righteousness.” He was counted righteous because he was strong in faith; he is the father of our faith.

Paul uses Abraham as the example to show us that we have to have faith in Christ, and that his death and sacrifice is what we need. We no longer need animals. If you put animals before Christ and the temple is gone, you have condemned yourself by default, with no animal to atone with and no priest or temple to atone in.

Israel was so accustomed to sacrificing animals that Paul said: fine, but make sure you acknowledge Christ and his sacrifice first. If you acknowledge Christ second, or not at all, and put your faith in that animal, you are done. You are in debt.

“Now it was not written for his sake alone, that it was imputed to him; But for us also, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead”. Not for Abraham alone, but for us. That is what we have to believe: we have to believe in Christ. The faith must come first.

“Who was delivered for our offences”: delivered, killed, for our offences. Our is a possessive word. “and was raised again for our justification”: raised from the dead for our justification, our reconciliation. Earlier Paul said Christ’s death justifies the ungodly.

Who is the our? Israel. And the many that are justified? Israel. When you read justification all through Paul’s letters, there should be no confusion about what he is talking about, or whom.

precepts.why:
Whose offences was Christ delivered for? “Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows”: our griefs are the same as our offences. This is Isaiah talking about his people. “But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed”: healed, delivered, saved.

You might think, no, that is other nations, that is everybody. Read on: “All we like sheep have gone astray”. Like sheep of what? The house of Israel. “and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.” Who is the us? The sheep.

“He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth”: he did not say one word. “He was taken from prison and from judgment: and who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off out of the land of the living”: he was killed. Keep this part in mind.

“for the transgression of my people was he stricken.” Not all people, not all nations, not the good nations, not the not-so-bad ones: my people. Isaiah was an Israelite. Now you know who the our is, who the all is and who the we is.

All the apologists have to do is show where this changed in the Old Testament, where Isaiah says, I almost forgot, and other nations too. It is not there. As Peter said, they wrest the other scriptures. This is where Paul got it: “delivered for our offences” is for his people.

“Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city”: 490 years, upon Daniel’s people. “to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins”: that is what Christ did when he died. “and to make reconciliation for iniquity”: reconciliation goes back to the word atonement and the word justification. “and to anoint the most Holy”: that is Christ.

Verse 25 is what must take place to fulfil verse 24: “from the going forth of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem”, the rebuilding in the Persian time, “unto the Messiah the Prince”, in the time of Rome.

“And after threescore and two weeks shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself”: he would be killed, but not for himself. For whom? His people. That is what Isaiah said: for the transgression of my people was he stricken. He would die for the transgressions, the offences, of his people.

“and the people of the prince that shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary”: that is Titus and Vespasian. “and the end thereof shall be with a flood, and unto the end of the war desolations are determined”: the war of 70 AD, and Israel removed out of the land and scattered among all nations into slavery. That is also the temple destroyed, so atoning with animals would come to an end.

“by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many”. By the Father’s knowledge, the righteous servant, Christ, shall justify many: give them justification. Some say, see, many means anybody. “for he shall bear their iniquities”: this goes back to the iniquity of us all, the sheep, in verse 6, and to my people in verse 8. The thought has not changed. The many are Israelites.

“Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great”: the kingdom, “and he shall divide the spoil with the strong”: the fellow heirs, us. “because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors”: the malefactors. “and he bare the sin of many”: he justified many.

“and made intercession for the transgressors.” Intercession makes him an intercessor, a mediator: someone that steps in and dies in your place, on your behalf. Nowhere in this chapter will you read other nations. There is no Isaiah 53 part two for other nations.

My righteous servant shall justify many: who are the many? “In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified”. Not all the seed of Israel and anybody else; not the good nations, the individual heathens that have black friends. All the seed of Israel: all twelve tribes shall be justified, and Christ justifies them by dying on the cross.

So “raised again for our justification” is the justification of the seed of Israel.

sense.text:
“Therefore being justified by faith”. Romans 5:1 continues from Romans 4:25, just as Romans 11 continues from the last two verses of Romans 10. Paul did not stop and start a new topic. The chapters and verses were added later, to find things faster; it was originally one long letter. That is why he begins with therefore.

Who, according to the Old Testament, would be justified? Israel. All the seed of Israel shall be justified; my righteous servant shall justify many, by dying for them, by laying on himself the iniquity of them all. Through the death of Christ we are justified by faith, not by animal sacrifice anymore.

“we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ”: through his body, not animals. What would come to pass, Daniel 9:24-26, is that the temple would be destroyed, so we could not atone with animals anymore. We had to have faith in Christ; otherwise you condemn yourself, indebted to a law you can no longer keep, with the priests scattered abroad and the temple destroyed with not one stone left standing.

precepts.why:
Isaiah 53 already said it: “But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities”. You know who the our is now: Israel. “the chastisement of our peace was upon him”: the chastisement on him was our peace with the Father. “and with his stripes we are healed”: healed from our iniquities.

That is the peace of Romans 5:1: we have peace with God because the chastisement of our peace was laid on Christ.

sense.text: “For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” Who did Christ die for? Who are the ungodly? Israel.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” The we that Christ died for, while we were yet sinners, is Israel.

“Much more then, being now justified by his blood”. What replaced the animals? His blood. The animals are the works we no longer receive justification from; by his blood we receive justification, atonement, reconciliation.

“we shall be saved from wrath through him.” The wrath is death, and we are saved from it through him, through his death.

“For if, when we were enemies”: Israelites were the enemies, “we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son”. When we were enemies to God, we were reconciled back to the Father through the death of his Son.

What does reconcile mean? To bring back together again. Emphasize the again. Ephesians 2:14-16 says he reconciles both unto God: the both are the southern and northern kingdoms. Was there a time in the Old Testament when all nations were with God together with Israel? No. God had one chosen people. Show where God had a bunch of nations that were his chosen people: never. So how could they be reconciled to him? They were not with him in the first place. Reconciliation does not fit other nations; that word destroys Christianity.

Who was with God before? We were. So when Christ died, we came back to him again. When were the Moabites joined with God? Never, so they cannot be reconciled with God. You cannot come together again with somebody you were never together with before. A couple were married, divorced, and reconciled; but reconciled when they were never married before? That don’t make no damn sense.

Christianity starts in the middle of Romans 5 where it is confusing. You have to start earlier, and hold on to these words, or Christianity will seep into your brain and have you lost.

“much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life.” Reconciled by his death, we will be saved through his life, the commandments of God as well.

“And not only so, but we also joy in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom we have now received the atonement.” Some Bibles have a word next to atonement: reconciliation. Reconcile in verse 10 and atonement in verse 11 are the same word. Christ died on the cross and atoned for us, and by dying for us he brought us back to the Father. That is also called adoption.

Atonement is reparation for a wrong or injury: when Christ died on the cross, he died for our wrongs and our injuries. The Christian theology sense, the reconciliation of God and all humankind, is nonsense, because God was never with all humankind. The word itself is at-one-ment. Who did God come to bring together as one? Israel, both kingdoms. It is joining the two sticks together: unity, unifying both kingdoms. All nations were never one with Israel. Ever.

Reconciliation is the restoration of a friendly relationship: reuniting, reunion, reconcilement, and propitiation, which is in the Bible too. It is full of peace: that is Isaiah 53 and Romans 5:1.

precepts.why:
This lines up exactly with Romans 5. “But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.” Christ came and died for his people; he was cut off for his people.

“For he is our peace, who hath made both one”. Who are the both? The two nations. They split apart; read the history in Kings. In Ezekiel it was prophesied that our king, Christ, would come and die for the nation of Israel and the nation of Judah, and they would no longer be two nations: he would make them one, one nation under Christ.

“and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us”, “for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace”: what was two is now one new man. “And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross”, so there would be no more division.

The audience is the same people he was talking to in the old covenant: the Jews in the church at Rome, and the Gentiles with them, the northern kingdom. That is the reconciliation of Romans 5, and it ties back to Romans 11.

What does it mean, “when we were enemies”? “But they rebelled, and vexed his holy Spirit”: that is us. We rebelled and vexed his holy spirit; we pissed God off. “therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and he fought against them.” He sent nations to beat us and overthrow us. That is when we were enemies, and that is who was reconciled to God by the death of his Son.

Atonement under the law: “But Aaron and his sons offered upon the altar of the burnt offering, and on the altar of incense, and were appointed for all the work of the place most holy, and to make an atonement for Israel”. Not for everybody: for Israel, “according to all that Moses the servant of God had commanded.” The atonement Christ made, which replaced that work, is for the same people.

“And they brought forth the he goats for the sin offering before the king and the congregation; and they laid their hands upon them: And the priests killed them, and they made reconciliation with their blood upon the altar, to make an atonement for all Israel”.

Reconciliation and atonement were made through animals, and when Christ died his body replaced them. Atonement, or at-one-ment, reconciliation and justification are three words that mean the same thing, for the same people, with the same God.

“for the king commanded that the burnt offering and the sin offering should be made for all Israel.” All means all twelve, because Hezekiah was trying to bring them back together: all twelve tribes, and the strangers of the people that came up for the Passover.

sense.text: “And not rather, (as we be slanderously reported, and as some affirm that we say,) Let us do evil, that good may come? whose damnation is just.” During his ministry Paul was slandered as teaching a false gospel, teaching against the law of Moses. Paul is referring to the Jews here. Their damnation for slandering him is just: they know that is not what he is saying, but they say it anyway.

“What then? are we better than they? No, in no wise”. These men slander us and their damnation is just, but are we better than them? No, because once upon a time Paul was them.

“for we have before proved both Jews and Gentiles, that they are all under sin”. Christians say: see, Jews and Gentiles, we are all under sin. But Paul says we have proved it. Where would you go to prove it? Not Paul’s letters: Paul was citing the law and the prophets. To prove that Jews and Gentiles are under sin, you must show the Gentiles under sin in the Old Testament, and if Gentiles means other nations, you cannot, because it is not there. Isaiah 53 says Christ bore the iniquity of Israel.

Show one nation by name, Moab, Ammon, Ishmael, that was under the old covenant with us and transgressed: not individuals, not the mixed multitude, but a nation God called his people along with Israel. You will not find it. The Gentiles were never under the covenant, so the Gentiles here cannot be other nations. They are Ephraim, the northern kingdom: Israelites. Both kingdoms went off and broke God’s covenant, as the history of the kings shows. Romans 11 and Acts 10 all come together.
“As it is written, There is none righteous, no, not one”. Paul goes on to prove it, citing the scriptures.

“There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God.” The context is proving that both Jews and Gentiles are under sin. Paul pulls the precepts, from David’s Psalms and so on, to show that all Israel went against the Lord and his commandments, that Judah and Israel were both sinful. In the eyes of God all twelve were evil as hell: not just the Jews, both kingdoms, Ephraim and Judah, were rebellious.

“They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable”. They all went off; they are all under sin. Together: both kingdoms were condemned, the southern kingdom and the northern kingdom, Judah and Ephraim, the one called Gentiles in this chapter. “there is none that doeth good, no, not one.”

“Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law”. Whatever the law says, and the Psalms and the prophets can be counted too, it says to them that are under the law. Who was under the law? Israel. So who are the Jews and Gentiles in verse 9? Israel.

Those under the law are the ones who break it, and when you break it you are under sin. Paul proved both Jews and Gentiles under sin, which means both Jews and Gentiles were under the law. The Gentiles cannot be other nations. It cannot be.

“that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God.” Who is the world here? Israel, because the whole world did not get God’s commandments under Moses at all.

“Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight”. What law is this? The law of sacrifice, because we are justified in Christ’s blood, as Romans 5 says.

“for by the law is the knowledge of sin.” When you broke God’s commandments, what did you have to do to acknowledge that you sinned, whether willfully or in ignorance? Offer up an animal. So by the law of sacrifice is the knowledge, the acknowledgment, of sin: you atoned for your knowledge of your sin with an animal.

precepts.why: Paul is quoting David: “They are all gone aside, they are all together become filthy: there is none that doeth good, no, not one.” David is talking about us, the nation of Israel. “There is none righteous” is Israel gone aside and become filthy.

We became filthy, and the atonement is reparation, whose root word is repair. “what shall I equal to thee, that I may comfort thee, O virgin daughter of Zion? for thy breach is great like the sea: who can heal thee?” A breach is a split, a tear. Who can heal the daughter of Zion? Our saviour, Christ.

“And the Lord shall guide thee continually, and satisfy thy soul in drought, and make fat thy bones: and thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not.” When our souls are in drought the Lord is going to water us and heal us.

“And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places”: the old waste places, because we became filthy. “thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.” That is the reparation right there: the repairer of the breach of Lamentations 2:13. The breach that is repaired is Israel’s.

“The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any that did understand, and seek God.” Read on and verse 3 answers: “They are all gone aside, they are all together become filthy: there is none that doeth good, no, not one.” David records it again, and that is what Paul quotes: “There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God.”

After “Their throat is an open sepulchre; with their tongues they have used deceit; the poison of asps is under their lips”, Paul cites Psalms 10: “His mouth is full of cursing and deceit and fraud: under his tongue is mischief and vanity.” That is us: the wicked of our people, and our enemies.

Paul quoted David; now he is quoting Isaiah. “Their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed innocent blood: their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity; wasting and destruction are in their paths. The way of peace they know not; and there is no judgment in their goings: they have made them crooked paths: whosoever goeth therein shall not know peace.” Isaiah is talking about Israelites here. Paul’s “Their feet are swift to shed blood” and “the way of peace have they not known” are Israel.
“There is no fear of God before their eyes” is from Psalms 36: “The transgression of the wicked saith within my heart, that there is no fear of God before his eyes.” That was us.

What is sin? “Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law.” Sin is the breaking of the law, and when you break God’s laws you are called a sinner.

So when Paul says “we have before proved both Jews and Gentiles, that they are all under sin”, he has pulled together the Psalms and Isaiah to show that all of us were evil as hell, wicked as hell together. To be under sin you have to have broken the law, so both Jews and Gentiles were under the law, and only Israel was under the law.

sense.text: They try to include the other nations in our restoration, our reconciliation. “Simeon hath declared how God at the first did visit the Gentiles, to take out of them a people for his name.” That is what took place in Acts 10, and it is Israel.

“After this I will return, and will build again the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down”. Build again: that is the reconciliation, the reparation, again. Fallen down: we became filthy, and the old waste places are restored. “and I will build again the ruins thereof, and I will set it up”. Who is that? All twelve tribes of Israel.

“That the residue of men might seek after the Lord”: the residue is Edom and the other nations, the rest outside the twelve tribes. “and all the Gentiles, upon whom my name is called, saith the Lord, who doeth all these things.” The Gentiles upon whom his name is called are the Christians, and the Jews. They try to include themselves in our reconciliation, our restoration and our adoption.

precepts.why:
James is quoting Amos: “In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof”. The breaches are the tear, the split: reparations, whose root word is repair. “and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old”.

“That they may possess the remnant of Edom, and of all the heathen, which are called by my name”. The twelve tribes possess the remnant of Edom and of all the heathen. So the residue of men and the Gentiles called by his name in Acts 15 are what Israel possesses. Other nations cannot be involved in our reconciliation, our restoration or our reparation.

sense.text:
“Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world”: Adam, “and death by sin”. Sin and death are synonymous, because the wages of sin is death; they go hand in hand. “and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned”.

That is where the Christians start: all have sinned. Who is the all? You read it earlier in Romans 3. Yes, Adam brought sin upon all men, and all nations are capable of sinning. Death did pass upon all men. The question is who God held accountable for the sins they committed.

What Paul is doing in Romans 5 is giving the origin of sin: how sin came into the world, and how Christ came after that to repair us and give us life.

“For until the law sin was in the world”: until the law of sacrifice under Moses, sin was in the world, because Adam brought it into the world. “but sin is not imputed when there is no law.” Imputed means charged, acknowledged. Sin is not imputed when there is no sacrifice. There always had to be a sacrifice of some kind to impute sin upon someone; sacrifice and death always went hand in hand.

“Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses”: the law here is Moses. “even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam’s transgression”: everybody did not sin the same way Adam sinned, but they sinned regardless. “who is the figure of him that was to come.” Adam was a similitude of Christ.

“But not as the offence, so also is the free gift.” Adam was like a Christ figure in the beginning, but Adam brought in the offence; Christ did not, Christ brought the opposite. Christ is the free gift.

“For if through the offence of one many be dead”: Adam brought death and destruction; paradise was removed from the earth, then the flood came. “much more the grace of God, and the gift by grace, which is by one man, Jesus Christ, hath abounded unto many.” The same way death abounded through Adam and spread, Christ’s death abounds and brings forth life. They parallel each other: one brought death upon the righteous chosen nation, and one brought life upon the chosen nation.

“And not as it was by one that sinned, so is the gift: for the judgment was by one to condemnation”: Adam brought condemnation, sin and death. “but the free gift is of many offences unto justification.” Whose offences? Israel’s. My righteous servant shall justify many; all the seed of Israel shall be justified.

Paul is giving the rundown of how sin came into the world and killed off the chosen people in the beginning, how they always came back to keep the commandments of God, and how Christ eventually came to die for the sins of that same chosen line. It is the origin story of sin, and why Christ had to come into the world and die for his people.

“For if by one man’s offence death reigned by one; much more they which receive abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness shall reign in life by one, Jesus Christ.” The same way Adam brought death and it reigned in many, Christ died on the cross and life reigned in many. It is the polar opposite.

“Therefore as by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation”: by Adam’s transgression death and sin came into the world. “even so by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life.” By Christ’s death. Who are the all men there? Israel, the same people Isaiah said would be justified.

“For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.” When Adam sinned he brought sin into all his children. All nations come out of Adam, and some of them had knowledge of the commandments of God. But whose sins did Christ die for? Who received God’s commandments? Who got the covenant? Israel.

Yes, all nations have sinned, and God does not like it. But he deals with a specific people, and he gave them specific laws. That is who Paul is talking to.

“Moreover the law entered, that the offence might abound.” The law was introduced so sin could be understood: thou shalt not covet, thou shalt not steal, thou shalt not commit adultery. We are by nature a wicked people, so the law entered to guide us, to expose and reveal the sin in us so we can fight it off.

“But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound”. When we keep God’s commandments and laws, we realize how much we need grace, because of the evil that is in us. We are going to make mistakes; we will rise, fall and stumble. So we need more grace than we got under Moses, because animals cannot atone for everything. Christ had to replace them.

“That as sin hath reigned unto death, even so might grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life by Jesus Christ our Lord.” Grace is mercy: the mercy there was none of under Moses, when he that despised Moses’ law died without mercy.

precepts.why:
Death did pass upon all men; but who did God hold accountable? “And gavest a body unto Adam without soul, which was the workmanship of thine hands, and didst breathe into him the breath of life”. “And unto him thou gavest commandment to love thy way: which he transgressed”: he broke the law. “and immediately thou appointedst death in him and in his generations, of whom came nations, tribes, people, and kindreds, out of number.” All that came from Adam had death in them. Adam brought forth everybody.

“And every people walked after their own will, and did wonderful things before thee, and despised thy commandments.” The evil that was in Adam passed on into all nations. Adam gave birth to the wicked, Cain and them, who are the devil by default, then the other nations, and then the righteous line, the sons of God.

“And again in process of time thou broughtest the flood upon those that dwelt in the world, and destroyedst them.” “as death was to Adam, so was the flood to these”: Adam’s sin caused destruction, and the flood destroyed the wicked.

“Nevertheless one of them thou leftest, namely, Noah with his household, of whom came all righteous men.” Out of Adam’s descendants there was a particular righteous line, from Seth: Enos, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, then Noah. That line kept righteousness; all of Adam’s other children went the hell off. Noah fathered Shem, Ham and Japheth. Were the Hamites and Japhethites righteous in God’s commandments? No. So all righteous men is Shem’s line. The sons of God are not new: we were sons of God before, we sinned and he killed us with water; we came back as Israelites, and he is going to destroy us with fire. There is always a righteous line God deals with.

“they began again to be more ungodly than the first. Now when they lived so wickedly before thee, thou didst choose thee a man from among them, whose name was Abraham. Him thou lovedst, and unto him only thou shewedst thy will”. Him only. Out of all the line Abraham came from, God gave his laws to Abraham only. There was always a line of people God dealt with that alone was given his laws: Noah kept them, Seth’s line kept them, and Israel only got God’s laws.

“This people are descended of the Chaldeans: And they sojourned heretofore in Mesopotamia, because they would not follow the gods of their fathers, which were in the land of Chaldea.” This is Abraham, in Mesopotamia, in Ur, before he went to the promised land. His father Terah was in idolatry, but Abraham was not.

“For they left the way of their ancestors, and worshipped the God of heaven, the God whom they knew”. Abraham left the way of Terah and his wicked ancestors and learned God’s will: God showed his will to Abraham only. “Then their God commanded them to depart from the place where they sojourned, and to go into the land of Chanaan”: right back to Abraham getting the promised land in Genesis 15.

Here is what Paul wrote in Romans 5, in Ezra. “And madest an everlasting covenant with him, promising him that thou wouldest never forsake his seed. And unto him thou gavest Isaac, and unto Isaac also thou gavest Jacob and Esau. As for Jacob, thou didst choose him to thee, and put by Esau”: he hated Esau and cast him aside. “and so Jacob became a great multitude.” It is always that special line God deals with, and when that line goes into sin, God brings destruction every time, because the sin is in us from Adam.

“thy glory went through four gates, of fire, and of earthquake, and of wind, and of cold; that thou mightest give the law unto the seed of Jacob, and diligence unto the generation of Israel.” The law was given to the seed of Jacob: they are the ones under that law.

“And yet tookest thou not away from them a wicked heart”: the same evil that was in Adam passed on to us, the righteous line. “For the first Adam bearing a wicked heart transgressed, and was overcome; and so be all they that are born of him.” That is what Paul says: by one man sin entered. “Thus infirmity was made permanent”, because we are covered in his flesh; the law was in the heart of the people, but “with the malignity of the root; so that the good departed away, and the evil abode still.”

It happened over and over: from Adam to Noah, to Abraham, to now, the righteous get God’s laws, go against them, destruction comes, they repent, and out of that line the righteous rise up again. A repeated cycle. “then didst thou raise thee up a servant, called David”, to build a city, and “they that inhabited the city forsook thee, And in all things did even as Adam and all his generations had done: for they also had a wicked heart”: idolatry, rebellion, transgressing the commandments. That is us. “And so thou gavest thy city over into the hands of thine enemies.”

So the accountability for sin fell on the righteous line, over and over again, with wickedness and righteousness always in the midst of it. That is the all upon whom death passed in Romans 5:12, as far as God holding them accountable.

What does “sin is not imputed when there is no law” mean? “And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.” Why almost all things? Because there were sins no animal could atone for. Almost all things are purged with blood by the law of sacrifice, and without the shedding of blood there is no remission, no atonement. So sin is not imputed where there is no sacrifice.
“Now where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin.” When Christ died, there was no more offering for sin: no more animals, no more sacrifices.

Romans 4:15 says what Romans 5:13 says. “Because the law worketh wrath”: another word for wrath is death. The law of sacrifice works death, because we are sinful by nature. “for where no law is, there is no transgression.” Where there is no sacrifice, there is no death, no sin imputed. Sacrifice and death always went hand in hand; that is why under Moses you died without mercy under two or three witnesses.

“the free gift is of many offences unto justification” goes back to Romans 4:25: “Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification.” Who is the our? Israel. Who are the many? Israel. Our and many are exactly us.

Justification of life. “Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren”: men and brethren, Israel. “that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins”: through Christ. “And by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.”

In Christ we are justified from all the things we could not be justified from under Moses, under sacrifice. Hebrews 9:22 said almost all things are purged with blood; Christ’s death purges everything. That is justification.

sense.text: “For whom he did foreknow”: foreknow means knew before. “he also did predestinate”, which goes back to knowing them before. “to be conformed to the image of his Son”: there is a particular people he knew before, who were going to be conformed to the image of his Son. “that he might be the firstborn among many brethren”: Christ is the firstborn, and then there are others, for lack of a better word firstfruits.

“Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called”: moreover, there is more than verse 29. Whom he foreknew he predestinated, and them he called to be the elect, as Peter wrote: elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father. “and whom he called, them he also justified”: justified through the blood of Christ, as in Romans 5. “and whom he justified, them he also glorified.”

This is why we came here: when God made Adam, there was a nation God already knew before they were made, and he said, I will have them justified through my son’s death and glorified. All nations received some form of law from Adam down, and they all sinned. But who did God predestinate? Israel. There is no getting around it in Romans 5. Yes, nations sin; but Christ was predestined to die for Israel, and Israel was predestined to be God’s people.

precepts.why:
“Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father”. These strangers are the elect. Foreknowledge is who you had knowledge of before; foreknew and foreknowledge are the same word. Whom he foreknew, he predestinated.

“through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ”: Christ’s death, as Romans 5 said.

“But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people”. Who is Peter writing to? The same strangers scattered abroad in chapter 1, throughout Galatia, the same people Paul wrote to in the book of Galatians: Israelites. They are the ones he foreknew and predestinated.

On foreknew: “Hear this word that the Lord hath spoken against you, O children of Israel, against the whole family which I brought up from the land of Egypt, saying, You only have I known of all the families of the earth”. You only have I known, or foreknew, of all the nations that came out of Adam.

“therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.” Not all nations that came out of Adam: you. All nations can sin, but God said, I only know you; I acknowledge your sins; I want you to stop sinning. The others he is going to destroy anyway. I am sending Christ to die for your sins, not everyone’s.

“Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” This goes back to reconcile, reconciliation: we cannot walk together unless both agree, and that is not all nations.

Them he justified are those he glorified, whom he foreknew. “In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified, and shall glory.” Who are we talking about? Israel. That is Romans 8:30 said by Isaiah: justified, and glorified.

sense.text: “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, to the saints which are at Ephesus, and to the faithful in Christ Jesus”. The same saints he wrote to at Rome.

“According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world”. God chose us before the earth was made. Before Adam was made, he said, this will be my people. So Adam and all nations, it does not matter: out of all nations, before the earth was formed, he made us and predestinated us to be his people.

He chose us in him: the same way Eve was in Adam, we were in Christ. We are the bride. “that we should be holy and without blame before him in love”: we, not everybody, should be holy.

“Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself”. Who is the us? Those whom he foreknew. The adoption goes back to the same words: reconciliation, justification, restoration, atonement. It is all the same thing. We will be the true God’s children because Christ died for us, if we overcome. “according to the good pleasure of his will.”

precepts.why: One more for the saints: “Gather my saints together unto me; those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice.” Did all nations make a covenant with God by sacrifice? No, they most certainly did not. So the saints at Ephesus, like the saints at Rome, are Israel.

On foreknew: “I say then, Hath God cast away his people?” Modern Christians say we were cast away because we denied Christ. “God forbid. For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.” “God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew.” Which he foreknew: back to Amos 3 and Romans 8. The people he foreknew, and predestinated unto the adoption, are Israel.

“For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh”. Paul says, I wish I could die for my people, my kinsmen: my race, ethnically, according to the flesh. “Who are Israelites”: Paul was of Benjamin.

“to whom pertaineth the adoption”: pertaineth means belongs. To Israel belongs the adoption of Ephesians 1:5, the atonement, the reconciliation, the justification, the restoration. “and the glory”: as Isaiah said, all the seed of Israel shall be justified and shall glory. “and the covenants”: who got the covenants? Israel, not all nations. “and the giving of the law”: who was under the law? Israel; whatever the law says, it says to them who are under the law. “and the service of God”: the servants of God, Israel. “and the promises”: the promises of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob belong to Israel.

“Whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came”: Christ came for Israel, “who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen.”
